blogs.title: The "Instigation" Problem in Fair Use: Does Commissioning a Work Preclude Transformative Use?
blogs.description: This post examines the Second Circuit's rejection of Santos's novel argument that Kimmel's use was not transformative because Kimmel "instigated" the creation of the videos and was thus the "designer" of their original purpose. The court's reliance on the Warhol objective standard—focusing on what a reasonable observer would think rather than the subjective intent of either party—clarifies that even when a secondary user commissions the original work, the transformative use inquiry remains an objective one. The post also addresses the court's treatment of Santos's bad faith argument based on Kimmel's use of fictitious names, the Supreme Court's apparent retreat from the Harper & Row "good faith" requirement, and the implications of resolving fair use at the pleading stage under Rule 12(b)(6).

blogs.title: Strategic Avoidance: The Second Circuit Sidesteps Copyright Preemption in Santos v. Kimmel
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Second Circuit's decision to avoid resolving whether Santos's breach of contract and implied contract claims were preempted by the Copyright Act, instead affirming their dismissal on state law grounds. The court's pragmatic approach—resolving claims on the narrowest available basis—raises broader questions about the development of copyright preemption doctrine. When courts sidestep preemption questions, they leave litigants without guidance on the boundary between copyright claims and state law contract claims involving creative works. The post situates this avoidance strategy within the broader landscape of Second Circuit preemption jurisprudence and considers when courts should confront preemption directly rather than reaching for alternative grounds for dismissal.

blogs.title: Platform Terms of Service and the Limits of Enforcement by Non-Parties
blogs.description: This post focuses on the court's dismissal of Santos's contract claims, which turned on his inability to enforce Cameo's Terms of Service as a non-party. The court's application of Illinois's strong presumption against third-party beneficiary status—reinforced by the fact that other provisions of the Terms of Service expressly included third-party beneficiary language—highlights a structural tension in platform ecosystems. Platform participants like Santos may rely on terms of service to govern user behavior but lack standing to enforce them. The post also examines the court's dismissal of Santos's implied contract claim for failure to plead essential terms and the fraudulent inducement claim for failure to allege out-of-pocket damages, discussing how these state law requirements function as independent barriers to relief for creators seeking redress for deceptive solicitation of their content.
